Evolution must have a pretty wild imagination. Somewhere along the way nature said, “Let’s make this one really confusing,” and somehow it worked perfectly. CNN.COM Birds and scientists are fooled by the ‘spider' on this viper's tail | CNN… Fuente: CNN.

item.title: Grass and clover can provide more than animal feed
item.description: Growing leys—grass and clover—is nothing new in Swedish agriculture. But in the arable farming regions dominated by cereal production, leys are less common. One reason is that there needs to be a market for what is harvested. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When prepping for disaster, don't forget to pack your teddy bear
item.description: Imagine it's the dead of night. Your phone pings with a text—it's a government emergency alert: "Leave your home immediately! Only take with you enough supplies for the next three days." What would you want in your go-bag? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Robots grow and package lettuce year-round in Norway's fully automated farm
item.description: Norway's first fully automated facility for vegetable production was put into operation last fall. This spring, the first products hit store shelves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Museums on prescription: How cultural activities are becoming crucial to the public health debate
item.description: On June 18, 2026, on the sidelines of the European Council in Brussels, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union signed a joint declaration making culture a strategic priority for the first time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Toxic algae can pose a hidden danger to dogs swimming in freshwater
item.description: Diving into cool water can be a quick way to escape the summer heat, but during certain times of year, freshwater can pose hidden dangers to people and pets. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From toothbrushes to aerospace: Graphene research advances fibers that conduct heat efficiently
item.description: KAIST's discovery of graphene oxide liquid crystals in 2011 laid the foundation for 15 years of research worldwide, leading to technologies for producing graphene fibers with high strength and thermal conductivity. The fundamental materials research that helped bring antibacterial toothbrushes and functional sportswear to market is now advancing into materials for thermal management. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Europe's earliest glacier loss day in years signals a reckoning for the Alps
item.description: On June 29, 2026, the snow accumulated by Switzerland's glaciers over the course of the previous winter had melted. Known as Glacier Loss Day, this date marks the point at which further melting begins to erode the glaciers' mass until snow accumulation resumes in the fall. Matthias Huss, the network head of Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS), told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that this year's Glacier Loss Day was "three months too early, compared to a healthy state." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossil plankton shells reveal reduced nitrogen fixation in warmer oceans 3 million years ago
item.description: Nitrogen is a key nutrient because it fuels the growth of plankton, which forms the basis of the marine food web. Two opposing processes determine the global nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation and denitrification. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Circular economy pilot projects show hotels can reduce waste and costs
item.description: The new EU Packaging Regulation (PPWR) has been in effect since Aug. 12, 2026. Under this regulation, beginning in January 2030, the food service industry may no longer buy food or toiletries packaged in single-use plastic—for example, ketchup packets or individually wrapped bars of soap. This is increasing pressure on hotels, restaurants and catering businesses to act. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cognitive resilience helps to predict Alzheimer’s dementia
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02897-4 The trait could explain why symptoms vary in severity between people with similar brain pathology. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Chinese companies doubled down on science after US tech restrictions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02946-y Affected Chinese companies adjusted their sources of knowledge to stay competitive. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoying You

item.title: A finely tuned mess—how disorder can make networks more stable
item.description: Perfection is overrated—at least when it comes to complex systems like the power grid, food webs and advanced materials. For decades, scientists generally assumed that networks function most reliably when their individual components are as similar as possible. But real-world networks are rarely uniform. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Developing new asymmetric catalytic reactions for the synthesis of complex molecules
item.description: Do Hyun Ryu's research team in the Department of Chemistry at Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) has developed two new asymmetric catalytic methods for the precise synthesis of complex molecules using chiral organic catalysts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ubiquitin marks abnormal glycogen for destruction to protect the brain, study finds
item.description: Researchers at the University of Cambridge and the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology have discovered a previously unknown cellular defense system that protects the brain from abnormal glycogen accumulation, which is linked to severe neurological disorders. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scaling up the detection of genome-edited rice lines
item.description: A new open-access study introduces RiSpy, a data-driven fingerprinting framework that makes the identification of genome-edited (GE) rice lines more robust, scalable and broadly applicable. Researchers from Sciensano, together with CIRAD and DARWIN project partners, in collaboration with colleagues from Ghent University, have presented the new methodological framework for the reliable identification of genome-edited (GE) rice lines in the journal Briefings in Bioinformatics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chemists overturn 40-year assumption about a key class of superconductors
item.description: Scientists at Warwick have shown that a material treated for 40 years as a uniform, textbook superconductor is in fact a patchwork of different crystal structures throughout its bulk, using an advanced 3D imaging technique to see deep inside the crystal for the first time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New krypton-88 data narrow a key gap in stellar strontium models
item.description: An international research team has reported the first experimental investigation of a nuclear physics reaction essential for understanding how the element strontium is produced in stars—specifically in stellar environments where traditional explanations for its formation fall short. The study, published June 8 in Communications Physics, reports that the team used indirect experimental techniques to extract previously inaccessible information about how an isotope of a separate element—krypton—absorbs, or captures, neutrons. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Transfer learning corrects alloy calculations to predict unexplored materials
item.description: Metals can be transformed into alloys by adding different elements, allowing their strength, stability and other properties to be tailored. A key parameter for understanding these properties is the volume size factor (VSF), which quantifies lattice distortion caused by differences in atomic size. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Motivational traits may help explain why some people report greater well-being
item.description: "People who are determined, passionate and believe in their ability to improve appear more likely to flourish and experience meaningful, engaging lives," says Professor Hermundur Sigmundsson at NTNU's Department of Psychology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newfound fungal nutrient-sensing mechanism could advance biofuels and disease control
item.description: Scientists have taken a step toward a better understanding of how fungi sense and respond to nutrients in the environment, which is critical for engineering fungi for green technologies and combating fungal pathogens and their resistance to treatments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China has gained pace in the space race by recovering rockets – but can it relaunch one?
item.description: As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the second part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Ben Jiang examine the country’s strategy and progress on reusable rockets – a field where the US has a tremendous lead. US commercial space firm SpaceX has been eager to tout its deployment of reusable first-stage rocket boosters, claiming to have flown more than 600 missions with the cost-cutting launch components. Despite... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Wency Chen,Ben Jiang

item.title: Why global wind energy may stay steady even as storm tracks shift poleward
item.description: Understanding how wind changes in response to global warming is necessary for accurately modeling climate and weather, identifying risks to infrastructure, and assessing global wind power capacity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Laser shocks turn plastic into ultra-small, high-purity nanodiamonds
item.description: Nanodiamonds are tiny diamond particles that usually measure mere millionths of a millimeter. They are extremely hard, stable and heat-resistant and highly adaptable for various purposes in medicine, new materials, catalysis and energy technology. By compressing plastic with lasers, researchers at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) and the University of Rostock are now able to systematically produce high-purity, ultra-small diamonds with a narrow size distribution. This is impossible to achieve with conventional methods such as explosions. As a scalable technology, laser… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trump administration overhauls key protection for endangered species
item.description: President Donald Trump's administration will no longer treat the unintentional killing of protected wildlife as unlawful, officials confirmed Thursday, in a shift conservationists say effectively guts the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Electron and photon beams drive same gold-forming reaction toward different nanoscale structures
item.description: Beauty and mystery—it is hard to imagine a more alluring combination, and this is precisely what we encounter when we observe phenomena in the nanoworld. But are we really sure that observations made using modern microscopic techniques do not influence what is happening there? A comparison of images of copper oxide nanoparticles reacting with chloroauric acid, obtained using electron and photon beams, has yielded unexpected results. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Microfluidic device simulates human tissue and offers an alternative to animal testing
item.description: Researchers at the Brazilian Center for Research in Energy and Materials (CNPEM) have developed microfluidic technology that can grow cells in three dimensions (3D). The goal is to conduct toxicity tests on new products by more accurately simulating living organisms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New bioinformatics tools help identify pathogenic variants in the genome
item.description: Structural variants and so-called tandem repeats are individual differences in the human genome. They are increasingly linked to diseases, but analyzing and interpreting them poses challenges for researchers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new rulebook for designing stable dilute alloy catalysts
item.description: Dilute alloy catalysts could improve fuel, plastic and pharmaceutical production, but their instability under heat holds back widespread use. Researchers at University of Michigan Engineering built a stability rulebook for this class of materials, which are made of a tiny amount of an active dopant metal dispersed in an inert host metal. A study outlining the rulebook was published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Close-up images show defects locking electrons into stable Wigner solids
item.description: A team of researchers led by the U.S. Department of Energy's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab) developed an approach that enabled them to directly observe how electrons interact with defects in advanced semiconductor devices in unprecedented detail. The team's methodology included an innovative simulation tool that enabled accurate theoretical interpretations of its experimental observations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How accurately can we measure the ocean's deepest point?
item.description: How deep is the deepest ocean—and how precisely can we actually measure it? A Japanese research team led by the National Institute of Polar Research (NIPR), SOKENDAI, the University of Tokyo and other Japanese institutions has mapped the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench using the EM124 multibeam echosounder aboard the research vessel Hakuho-maru. Their study is published in the journal Scientific Data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This sponge has holes. Some find that truly disgusting
item.description: Imagine you're scrolling through TikTok and come across an image of a lotus seed pod or sponge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Disorder is key to tuning a high-temperature superconductor
item.description: Cornell physicists have discovered that minimizing disorder, not varying electron count, is the key factor for controlling superconductivity in the unique material iron selenide (FeSe), a new insight for understanding high-temperature superconductors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Awards Launch Services for StarBurst Gamma-Ray Detector
item.description: NASA has selected SpaceX to provide launch services for the agency’s StarBurst mission, a small satellite designed to investigate neutron star mergers and the origins of short gamma-ray bursts. StarBurst will launch aboard a Bandwagon rideshare mission on a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: A new bridge for quantum networks: Physicists convert microwaves to light using 2D magnets
item.description: Physicists at The City College of New York have demonstrated a new way to transfer microwave signals onto light using magnetic waves inside a layered semiconductor. The work establishes a materials platform for building interfaces that could one day link quantum computers through optical networks. The research, titled "Microwave-to-optical transduction using magnon–exciton coupling," was led by the Laboratory for Nano and Micro Photonics (LaNMP) at CCNY, headed by physics professor Vinod M. Menon. It appears in the journal Nature Materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Moles' wide-armed posture reshapes how their shoulder bones carry loads
item.description: While the scapula is the primary bone supporting the body in terrestrial quadrupedal mammals, an analysis of internal bone structure in underground moles (family Talpidae) showed a more important role for the clavicle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global water report reveals drying rivers and erratic swings between too little and too much
item.description: Rivers across the globe in 2025 had one of the driest years in more than three decades, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). It shows a continuation of the long-term decline in Earth's freshwater storage and glacier retreat—trends with serious implications for people and economies in the future. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El despegue de la India: el tercer mercado aeroespacial del mundo
item.description: El sector de la aviación civil en la India atraviesa su etapa de mayor auge. En la última década, el país ha construido más de 70 nuevos aeropuertos y ya supera los 400 millones de pasajeros anuales, consolidándose como el tercer mercado de aviación más grande del planeta, solo por detrás de Estados Unidos y China. Un informe de Alban Alvarez, Sacha Desmaizières y Supriya Kumar para France 24. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: Alban Alvarez

item.title: Decoding the DNA switches behind gene regulation
item.description: Understanding gene regulation may be key to interpreting human disease genetics. Genes are regulated in part by stretches of DNA called enhancers, which define when, where and how strongly each gene is turned on. Mapping enhancers and how they function in specific cell types is necessary for understanding gene regulation and disease-related genetic variants. But the location and activity of enhancers are highly cell type-specific, making it difficult to accurately predict enhancer–gene interactions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Small portfolio shifts could deliver major food sustainability gains, UK analysis finds
item.description: Leading UK food and drink manufacturers could significantly improve the overall nutrition and sustainability of their products by making changes to 10% or less of their existing product line, according to new research in Nature Food. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Vapor-phase synthesis of MXenes could expand their technological applications
item.description: MXenes are two-dimensional nanomaterials first synthesized at Drexel University in 2011. They have been recognized by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry as an emerging technology with "true potential to transform our world." But their widespread use has thus far been limited by the complicated process required to produce them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Using sound waves to turn iron and water into magnetic nanoparticles
item.description: Iron rusts on its own, slowly, over months or years. Now, researchers at Tohoku University have found a way to compress the process of metal reacting with water to form oxide, taking mere hours and using nothing more than ultrasound. Details were published in the journal Ultrasonics Sonochemistry. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New study explores US consumers' willingness to pay for fresh-market grape attributes
item.description: A recent study examined U.S. consumers' preferences and willingness to pay for different attributes of fresh-market grapes, providing insights for growers, retailers and the fresh produce industry. The research evaluated how factors such as grape size, sweetness, seedlessness, color and production methods influence purchasing decisions. Findings reveal that certain attributes significantly affect consumer buying behavior, offering guidance on which traits could be emphasized to meet market demand and potentially increase sales. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Portable metasurface biosensor turns molecular signals into images, bypassing spectrometers
item.description: What if signs of disease could be detected using nothing more than a tiny chip that fits in the palm of your hand and a camera, without ever visiting a hospital? A scene that once seemed possible only in science fiction has now moved one step closer to reality. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The AI Superintelligence Slowdown
item.description: Remember when tech leaders would tell their employees to “move fast and break things”? It seemed that would be the way of AI too. But after a summer where rogue AI agents became reality, and researchers warned that AI could kill us all, a number of leading US AI companies are publicly suggesting it’s time […] Fuente: The Verge.
item.dc:creator: Sean Hollister

item.title: Tons of fishing gear and plastic are washing up on Seychelles beaches. We tracked where it was coming from
item.description: Vast quantities of plastic and fishing gear are washing up along the shores of the Seychelles, destroying fragile ecosystems and causing significant economic problems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Two spike 'keys' work together to let SARS-CoV-2 enter cells, study reveals
item.description: To enter cells, the COVID-19 virus fuses its surrounding membrane with the membrane of the target cell. This is where the fusion peptides of the spike protein come into play. These regions function as molecular keys that allow the virus to open the door to the target cell and initiate fusion between the two membranes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Activated learning-and-memory protein forms growing molecular chains, imaging reveals
item.description: Researchers at the Nano Life Science Institute (WPI-NanoLSI) at Kanazawa University, Kyoto University, SOKENDAI and the National Institute for Physiological Sciences have revealed how CaMKIIα—a key brain protein involved in learning and memory—organizes itself into chain-like structures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: No hacían falta hipótesis exóticas para explicar los puntos rojos del James Webb. Solo la simulación más precisa jamás hecha del universo temprano
item.description: Poco después de comenzar con su trabajo de observación, el Telescopio Espacial James Webb detectó algo que ha traído de cabeza a astrónomos de todo el mundo desde entonces. Se trata de una serie de puntos rojos que parecen corresponderse con un objeto tan masivo y compacto que no debería existir según el modelo cosmológico actual. Desde finales de 2022, cuando el telescopio arrojó las primeras imágenes de estos puntos rojos, se han lanzado varias hipótesis. Sin embargo, la mayoría de ellas tenían alguna laguna que impedía que cuadrasen por completo . Ahora, gracias a una supercomputadora… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: What kills Schrödinger's cat? Underground experiment rules out gravity model for quantum decoherence
item.description: Somewhere between the microscopic realm of elementary particles and the macroscopic world of human beings, something strange happens: The rules of quantum physics, which work so exquisitely for tiny atoms, seem to lose their grip as objects grow larger. Pondering where and how this shift from small-scale quantum fuzziness to everyday sharp certainty happens gives rise to thought-experiment oddities like Schrödinger's famous dead-and-alive cat. The process by which quantum phenomena like superposition—the paradoxical affliction of Schrödinger's cat—fade into the classical reality we experience… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What Wendell Berry meant to Christian farmers going green
item.description: In the late evening of Aug. 31, 2026, I missed a call from Jennifer, a seventh-generation cattle rancher in Georgia. She was one of more than 70 family farmers and ranchers across the rural U.S. South and Midwest whom I'd gotten to know through my research over the past five years. We still kept up from time to time, but a late-night call had me worried that something had gone awry on her farm. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers who analysed 10,000 crashes say car size does matter
item.description: A study of 13 years of crashes in Australia finds a link between car height and risk of pedestrian death, particularly for women and children. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Andie Noonan, Margaret Burin, Joshua Byrd, Emma Machan, and Cristen Tilley

item.title: A glimpse of the solar system's origins: Striking details on the molecules inside a meteorite
item.description: Researchers at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory and Brookhaven National Laboratory have teamed up to get a fresh look at the complex makeup of meteorites and glimpse into our solar system's past. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How much do financial institutions really care about relationships?
item.description: How do you measure the value of a relationship? One way is forbearance—what the involved parties would give up to stay together. That's the principle used by Stephen Karolyi, associate professor of finance at the Costello College of Business at George Mason University, in his co-authored research on relationship lending in the banking industry. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Invites Media to SpaceX’s 35th Resupply Launch to Space Station
item.description: Media accreditation is open for the next cargo launch that will deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. The 35th SpaceX commercial resupply services mission to the orbital laboratory for NASA will lift off on a Falcon 9 rocket. NASA and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than October to launch […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lauren E. Low

item.title: Threatened bumblebee populations in England and Wales face severe genetic declines
item.description: A new study reveals that an important pollinator is rapidly losing genetic diversity in Britain. Moss carder bumblebees were once widespread across the UK, living in flower-rich meadows, marshes and heathlands, where they pollinated a wide variety of plants. However, the loss of these habitats has caused the species to retreat into strongholds along the country's coasts and islands. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 94 mil reproducciones · 1346 reacciones | New cat alert! A call from a wildlife sanctuary about a "weird cat" has led to the first new cat species discovered in over 100 years. Smaller than an average housecat and covered in leopard-like spots, the cat species—proposed name Leopardus tilcayo—lives in Bolivia’s Yungas forest ecoregion, and very little is known about its day-to-day life in the wild. Its discovery is redrawing the branches of the cat family tree, and researchers hope the methods used to identify it could be used to find even more new cat species around the world: https://on.natgeo.com/INjRv5 | National Geographic

item.title: Children from armed forces families have extra educational challenges
item.description: Service children are children of current or former armed forces personnel. Being a service child can be a source of pride, resilience and determination. Yet service life brings experiences and challenges their civilian peers may not face. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Real-time quantum jump in sound observed for first time
item.description: A Stanford team has documented the first direct observation of quantum jumps of sound in a mechanical resonator, completing an arc of scientific exploration that started more than 100 years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Virtual biotech company puts thousands of AI scientist agents to work on drug discovery
item.description: The latest company to spin out of a Stanford Medicine lab is a biotech undertaking with 37,000 employees—and none of them are human. There's no lab space, no lunch breaks and no payroll. It's an artificial intelligence-powered virtual biotech company that's the brainchild of associate professor of biomedical data science James Zou, Ph.D., who is also the principal investigator of a virtual lab that launched in 2025, and graduate student Harrison Zhang. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US sanctions boost China’s science-driven innovation by over 70%, study finds
item.description: US-sanctioned Chinese companies are increasingly turning to open-source research to innovate and reverse-engineer restricted foreign technology, with a 72 per cent surge in scientific literature citations in their patent applications, according to a new study. While the United States said it expanded its Entity List to safeguard national security and preserve its technological edge, an analysis of Chinese patent filings over the 12 years until 2022 showed that US restrictions on access to... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Holly Chik

item.title: Why the places we love in books can never quite be found in real life
item.description: From the Brontës' Haworth to Jane Austen's Bath, Wordsworth's Lake District and Thomas Hardy's Dorset, literary places continue to exert a powerful hold over readers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Marine carbon dioxide removal is advancing, but questions remain about viability, says new digital report
item.description: Marine carbon dioxide removal (CDR) has advanced significantly, with growing research activity, technological development, private-sector involvement and movement toward field testing. But major questions remain about whether these approaches can remove carbon dioxide at meaningful scales, how that removal can be reliably measured and verified, potential environmental effects, and how marine CDR should be governed, says a new digital report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a simple game of 20 questions could help make AI fit for the future
item.description: Artificial intelligence programs used to classify images could be trained much more cheaply using a surprisingly simple method inspired by the childhood game of 20 Questions, according to new research posted to the arXiv preprint server by a team from the University of Bristol. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nullarbor mapping reveals surface signs of deep, hidden cave systems
item.description: Mysterious trenches stretching for kilometers across southern Australia's Nullarbor Plain have been revealed as the surface footprints of deep, hidden ancient cave systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study maps where humans drive harmful nutrient levels along coasts
item.description: Along a quarter of the planet's coastal waterways, humans contribute more harmful nitrogen—via agricultural runoff, wastewater discharges and other activities—than all natural sources combined. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New benchmark puts quantum computers to the test and reveals their limitations
item.description: Quantum computers are no longer theoretical concepts. Today, they are being developed to tackle a range of complex problems, including exploring financial risk, modeling complex molecules and optimizing massive logistics networks. However, until now, there has been no way to benchmark the computational power of different systems on the same scale to see how they compare. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What ancient Mars rocks reveal about its buried carbonate stores
item.description: Carbonate minerals are among the best records of past liquid water on Mars: They form when water carrying dissolved carbon dioxide reacts with rock, and their composition reflects the chemistry of both. Yet Mars has surprisingly little carbonate on its surface compared with what climate models predict, given that the planet likely had a (at least transiently) thick, CO2-rich atmosphere more than 3 billion years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Opt-out AI training plan could weaken Australian copyright protections
item.description: The ground is shifting beneath the feet of Australian authors and other creatives. A leaked proposal seen by the ABC suggests the government might grant artificial intelligence (AI) companies access to the copyrighted works of Australians under an opt-out system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sixteen new fungus species found hiding in Thailand's flowers
item.description: Researchers have discovered 16 new species of fungus living unnoticed inside garden flowers and wildflowers across northern Thailand, more than quintupling the number of such fungi known to occur in the country. The findings are published in the journal IMA Fungus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Capybaras in the desert? Fossil casts doubt on Atacama as world's oldest continuously dry region
item.description: Ask any zoo-goer and they will tell you that capybaras are adorable. Ask a scientist specializing in the rodents, which resemble oversized guinea pigs, and they will tell you they are obligate semiaquatic herbivores that indicate persistent riparian ecosystems. In plain English: Capybaras like it wet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep-sea hydrothermal vents may be a hot spot for pregnant Antarctic krill
item.description: Antarctic krill are tiny shrimp-like creatures that were previously thought to mostly inhabit the upper layer of the Southern Ocean. Although they had occasionally been observed at deeper levels, they were never seen near deep-sea hydrothermal vents until 2024, when a group of oceanographers observed them there for the first time. The team's new study, published in Communications Biology, describes the discovery and why the team thinks pregnant krill may actually be spending a lot of time near hydrothermal vents. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why does laundry get smelly if it stays wet? A textile scientist explains how to fix it
item.description: You forget a load in the machine overnight, and by morning it smells worse than before you washed it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La órbita terrestre es un basurero: 17.000 toneladas de chatarra rodean la Tierra
item.description: La Agencia Espacial Europea contabilizó al 31 de julio, 46.870 objetos artificiales en órbita "detectables". Es decir, hay muchos más. Hay unos 230 millones de fragmentos de menos de un centímetro, que -a la velocidad que vuelan- son un peligro. Fuente: Clarín - Mundo.
item.dc:creator: Clarin.com - Home

item.title: Japanese supercomputer simulations may explain Webb's Little Red Dots
item.description: Of all the discoveries from the James Webb Space Telescope, the multitude of Little Red Dots it has observed is among the most enigmatic. Now, simulations using the Japanese Supercomputer ATERUI III have explained the nature of the Little Red Dots without requiring any exotic assumptions. The simulations show that the Little Red Dots are black holes growing at a rate that would be impossible today because of conditions in the early universe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: European ash pangenome could help researchers breed a generation of trees resistant to ash dieback
item.description: In a study published in the journal Nature Communications, researchers from the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Forest Research and collaborating organizations present the first-ever European ash (Fraxinus excelsior) pangenome, using high-quality DNA to aid research into natural ash dieback resistance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Diamond quantum sensors can detect heart magnetism at room temperature without skin contact
item.description: Physicists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) have developed a technology that uses quantum sensors to measure biomagnetic signals, such as heart activity. Researchers from the DIAQNOS (DIAmond-based Quantum Sensing for NeurOSurgery) flagship project, coordinated by Dr. Arne Wickenbrock in Mainz, have demonstrated the potential of quantum technology for future medical applications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Education reform student and professor find that social media also affects students in developing countries
item.description: Sometimes the best collaborations start with disagreements in class discussions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Black holes from stellar to supermassive size may follow one jet-launching rule
item.description: An early-career Western Australian astrophysicist has helped uncover a universal rule behind one of the most powerful behaviors in the universe: when black holes launch jets. The discovery, published in the journal Nature Astronomy, shows black holes appear to fire off powerful jets at the same critical point in their feeding cycle—whether they are about 10 times the mass of the sun or millions of times heavier. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Unveils Enterprise, the First Space Shuttle
item.description: Fifty years ago, on Sept. 17, 1976—Constitution Day of America’s bicentennial year—NASA unveiled its first space shuttle orbiter, OV-101, to the public. NASA had originally planned to name the vehicle Constitution, but a letter-writing campaign changed the agency’s plans. Nearly 100,000 fans of the Star Trek television series wrote the White House urging that the […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: El Niño may lift Australian food prices as dry conditions squeeze farms
item.description: Australia's farm sector currently faces a double whammy from weather and nonweather-related factors: a confirmed El Niño effect and surging inflationary pressures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wild honeybee populations in the EU are on the Red List for the first time
item.description: Populations of the Western honeybee (Apis mellifera) are under immense pressure in the wild in Europe. New research published in Conservation Science and Practice from the University of Hohenheim in Stuttgart and Agroscope in Zürich shows that there are frequent occurrences of honeybees in the wild in Europe. However, the researchers estimate that the populations of these bee populations in the European Union (EU) will fall by about 56% within 10 years without the influx of swarms from beekeepers. Therefore, wild honeybees are now officially classified as "endangered" across the EU on the… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nebraskans wary of risks surrounding artificial intelligence
item.description: Americans are grappling with artificial intelligence—from its lightning-fast development to the construction of data centers to support it—and are becoming more skeptical of its benefits. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Endurance running or endurance diving—which came first?
item.description: A new study combines paleoanthropology and diving physiology to address a fundamental question in human evolution: Why did humans evolve their exceptional aerobic endurance? Did our ancestors begin endurance running to exhaust terrestrial prey, or did breath-hold diving for aquatic resources also play a key role? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep-sea crustaceans caught hitching rides on giant sea spiders
item.description: Some types of marine life appear to have it easy. While exploring thousands of meters below the waves in the Chilean Margin in the southeastern Pacific Ocean, scientists observed tiny shrimp-like crustaceans known as amphipods (Mesopleustes abyssorum) clinging tightly to much larger giant sea spiders (Colossendeis colossea) that were scuttling on the ocean floor. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This popular fermented food may help flush nanoplastics from the body
item.description: A kimchi-derived bacterium can bind to nanoplastics under gut-like conditions and may help carry them out of the body. In mice, the probiotic more than doubled the amount of nanoplastics detected in feces, pointing to a surprising potential use for microbes from fermented foods. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: AI is shaping kids. What if kids could shape AI, too?
item.description: Vanderbilt University's Golnaz Arastoopour Irgens, assistant professor of human-centered learning technologies at Peabody College of Education and Human Development, partnered with Sarah K. Burriss (Ph.D. '23, Peabody's Department of Teaching and Learning), assistant professor of the practice at the College of Connected Computing, to rethink how kids should learn about artificial intelligence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Robotic lab sets up and runs optics experiments on demand
item.description: Every new generation of phone display, television screen and solar panel is the result of precision optics experiments, which use lasers and other light sources to measure the optical properties of candidate materials. These experiments can take months to run, requiring scientists to meticulously angle and adjust delicate light sources, mirrors, cameras and other components in a process of careful, constant tuning that can be physically tedious and time-consuming. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: "They should fly their capsule. The government paid a lot of money for that." Fuente: Ars Technica.

item.description: Se habla mucho sobre el papel de la misión DART , de la NASA, en el ensayo de técnicas dirigidas a la defensa planetaria. Sin embargo, otras compañías a las que quizás se ha dado menos publicidad han emprendido misiones similares. Es, por ejemplo, el caso de la Agencia Espacial Europea (ESA) con la misión Hera . item.title: A $100 detector can see invisible particles raining down from space
item.description: A pocket-sized, roughly $100 detector can reveal the invisible stream of cosmic particles constantly passing through Earth and even through our bodies. What began as a student physics project is now being used in major experiments, balloon missions, and potentially future spacecraft. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Laser scans reveal 23 hidden ship carvings on Bronze Age temple wall in Cyprus
item.description: About 40 years ago, researchers found ancient ship carvings on a temple wall in Cyprus, possibly all carved at once at the tail end of the Bronze Age, around the time of the infamous Bronze Age collapse. Then, decades later, a new study revealed they had missed nearly two dozen ancient carvings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What major tests like PISA and NAPLAN get wrong about Indigenous students
item.description: We've just received the results of the latest PISA test—the international assessment of 15-year-olds' science, math and reading skills. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astronomers just found the youngest known planet ever
item.description: Astronomers have confirmed a Jupiter-size planet less than a million years old, making Elias 2-24 b the youngest known planet and giving scientists a rare look at a world still being born. Its surprisingly rapid formation challenges leading theories about how giant planets come together, especially so far from their stars. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: More short holidays close to home boost well-being, study finds
item.description: Travel plays a far more critical role in mental health and well-being than previously thought, according to new University of the Sunshine Coast-led research. The study found frequent leisure travel boosts happiness, psychological resilience and overall quality of life, with the greatest benefits experienced by people who feel vulnerable or struggle to manage stress. Fuente: Phys.org.
